title: The Balance Sheet Equation
context: Analyze how the balance sheet equation requires total assets to equal the sum of total liabilities and total equity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A pallet loader used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
A pallet loader held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as a non-current asset because the dealer is a business rather than a household.
A pallet loader kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
The same pallet loader must always be classified identically on every balance sheet regardless of how it is held.
The same pallet loader may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
tactical_explanations:
Physical form alone does not make a pallet loader inventory. Inventory is held for sale or for cycle consumption — not every machine the firm owns.

Operating use beyond a year puts pallet loader among non-current tangibles. Counterexample: a forklift in the firm’s own warehouse is plant, not stock.

So the statement is False.

A dealer’s pallet loader held for customers is merchandise.

So the statement is False.

Multi-year operating use of a pallet loader fits the non-current tangible test.

Useful life beyond the period plus own use — not resale — drive that line.

Tangible means physical substance; non-current means long-term benefit.

Ask whether the reporter uses the object or holds it for sale.

Benefit lasting beyond one year points non-current; trading-cycle stock points current. Physical durability never overrides that use-versus-resale split. The wording lines up with that rule, so the assertion stands.

So the statement is True.

The same pallet loader need not share one balance-sheet line everywhere. Each reporter classifies by how it holds the object.

Operator → non-current tangible; dealer → inventory. Physical identity does not freeze the category.

So the statement is False.

Intended use decides the line for the same physical object.

So the statement is True.

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Non-current assets normally have a useful life of more than one year and are intended to be used in the business for longer than one year.
Non-current liabilities amount to less than 56.8% of total equity in Year 2.
The combined total of equity and non-current liabilities exceeds non-current assets by more than 7.3% in Year 1.

tactical_explanations:
Non-current assets are held for use beyond one accounting period.

Useful life beyond a year plus operating intent define the category.

Ask whether the reporter uses the object or holds it for sale.

Benefit lasting beyond one year points non-current; trading-cycle stock points current. Physical durability never overrides that use-versus-resale split. The wording lines up with that rule, so the assertion stands.

So the statement is True.

NCL-to-equity share = non-current liabilities ÷ total equity.

Name the ratio in words: non-current liabilities as a percentage of total equity.

$$
\text{NCL share} = \frac{\text{non-current liabilities}}{\text{total equity}}
$$

Non-current liabilities combine the long-term loan and bonds lines:

From the extract: Equity = 839.

$$
\text{NCL} = 220 + 63 = 283
$$

$$
\frac{283}{839} \approx 0.3373 \approx 33.7\%
$$

Year 2 NCL/equity is 33.7%, which is consistent with “less than 56.8%”. So the arithmetic supports the claim.

So the statement is True.

Long-term financing surplus = (equity + non-current liabilities) ÷ non-current assets − 1.

Name the identity in words: surplus of long-term financing over non-current assets.

$$
\text{Surplus} = \frac{\text{equity} + \text{NCL}}{\text{NCA}} - 1
$$

From the extract: NCA = 740.

$$
\text{Equity} + \text{NCL} = 761 + 267 = 1{,}028
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} \approx 1.3892
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} - 1 \approx 0.3892 \approx 38.9\%
$$

the surplus is 38.9%, which exceeds 7.3%. So the arithmetic supports the claim.

So the statement is True.

Percentage growth for Total equity is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

Name the growth identity in words.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{Y_1}
$$

From the extract: Y_1 = 761, Y_2 = 839.

$$
Y_2 - Y_1 = 839 - 761 = 78
$$

$$
\frac{78}{761} \approx 0.1025 \approx 10.2\%
$$

The claim wants growth of more than 24.5%.

actual growth is 10.2%, which is not more than the claimed 24.5%. So the arithmetic misses the claim.

So the statement is False.

Percentage growth for Total assets is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

Name the growth identity in words.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{Y_1}
$$

From the extract: Y_1 = 1,181, Y_2 = 1,279.

$$
Y_2 - Y_1 = 1{,}279 - 1{,}181 = 98
$$

$$
\frac{98}{1{,}181} \approx 0.0830 \approx 8.3\%
$$

The claim wants growth of more than 10%.

actual growth is 8.3%, which is not more than the claimed 10%. So the arithmetic misses the claim.

So the statement is False.

Consider the following two-year cash flow statement extract (in € thousands) for a business whose identity is not disclosed.

[[CHART type="bar" title="Operating and investing cash flows"]]
Year 1 | Operating=388 | Investing=-252
Year 2 | Operating=416 | Investing=-307
[[/CHART]]

| Item (€ thousands) | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cash flow from operating activities | 388 | 416 |
| Cash flow from investing activities | (252) | (307) |
| Dividends paid | (45) | (65) |
| Proceeds from new borrowing | 78 | 69 |
| Cash flow from financing activities | 33 | 4 |

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Dividends paid to shareholders are recorded within cash flow from financing activities, not cash flow from operating activities.
Cash flow from operating activities grew by more than 23.2% from Year 1 to Year 2.
If revenues exceed costs and expenses, the company has a profit; if costs and expenses exceed revenue, it suffers a loss.
Land is depreciated on a straight-line basis just like buildings and machinery.
Purchase of office equipment for cash is classified as an operating cash outflow.
tactical_explanations:
Dividends paid belong in financing activities.

They return cash to equity providers, not to the trading cycle. Operating cash is customers and suppliers; dividends are owner distributions.

So the statement is True.

Percentage growth for Cash flow from operating activities is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

Name the growth identity in words.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{Y_1}
$$

From the extract: Y_1 = 388, Y_2 = 416.

$$
Y_2 - Y_1 = 416 - 388 = 28
$$

$$
\frac{28}{388} \approx 0.0722 \approx 7.2\%
$$

The claim wants growth of more than 23.2%.

actual growth is 7.2%, which is not more than the claimed 23.2%. So the arithmetic misses the claim.

So the statement is False.

Profit means revenues exceed costs and expenses for the period.

The opposite gap is a loss.

So the statement is True.

Land is not depreciated like buildings and machinery.

It ordinarily has an indefinite useful life.

Counterexample: a factory plot stays at cost while the building is written down.

Straight-line thinking spreads (cost − residual) over useful life.

Land ordinarily skips that charge because its useful life is treated as indefinite. Cash left when the asset was bought; the later expense is an allocation, not a fresh outflow. State the corrected line or figure and the false claim has nowhere left to stand.

So the statement is False.

Buying office equipment for cash is an investing outflow.

So the statement is False.

Depreciation spreads depreciable cost over useful life.

It is normally non-cash; land is not depreciated like buildings. Against that rule the claim is right.

So the statement is True.

Depreciation spreads depreciable cost over useful life.

So the statement is True.

Revenue and costs are period flows; assets and liabilities are stocks.

With that split the claim is fine.

tactical_explanations:
Sort the movement into operating, investing, or financing.

So the statement is True.

Straight-line annual charge for each asset is (cost − residual) ÷ useful life; sum the three charges.

Name the identity in words: annual charge = (cost − residual) ÷ life; combined = sum of charges.

$$
\text{Asset A – Machinery}:
124{,}000 - 0 = 124{,}000
\frac{124{,}000}{11} \approx 11{,}273
$$

$$
\text{Asset B – Delivery truck}:
46{,}000 - 4{,}000 = 42{,}000
\frac{42{,}000}{6} \approx 7{,}000
$$

$$
\text{Asset C – Computer equipment}:
18{,}000 - 0 = 18{,}000
\frac{18{,}000}{3} \approx 6{,}000
$$

From the extract: Combined = 24,273.

Claimed €24,273. Actual ≈ €24,273.

combined charge ≈ €24,273 versus claimed €24,273 So the arithmetic supports the claim.

So the statement is True.

With nil residual, the asset is fully written down once elapsed years reach useful life.

From the extract: Cost = €18,000, Life = 3 years, Residual = €0.

After 3 years: fully written down to nil.

3 years ≥ life 3 with residual 0 So the arithmetic supports the claim.

Sum each asset's carrying value after three years (floored at residual once fully depreciated).

Name the identity in words: combined BV = sum of each asset's cost − min(3, life) × annual charge (at residual if fully depreciated).

$$
\text{Asset A – Machinery}\ BV_{3} = 90{,}182
$$

$$
\text{Asset B – Delivery truck}\ BV_{3} = 25{,}000
$$

$$
\text{Asset C – Computer equipment}\ BV_{3} = 0
$$

$$
\text{Combined BV} \approx €115{,}182
$$

Threshold: exceeds €106,072.

combined BV ≈ €115,182 versus exceeds €106,072 So the arithmetic supports the claim.

So the statement is True.

Carrying value after three years subtracts three annual charges from cost.

Name the identity in words: carrying value = cost − years elapsed × annual charge.

$$
46{,}000 - 4{,}000 = 42{,}000
$$

$$
\frac{42{,}000}{6} \approx 7{,}000
$$

$$
BV_{3} = 46{,}000 - 3 \times 7{,}000 = 25{,}000
$$

Claimed €28,880. Actual ≈ €25,000.

carrying value ≈ €25,000 versus claimed €28,880 So the arithmetic misses the claim.

So the statement is False.

$$
\text{Acid-test} = \frac{\text{current assets} - \text{inventory}}{\text{current liabilities}}
$$

$$
\text{CA} - \text{Inventory} = 276 - 119 = 157
